content: This is an updated version of the original Cochrane Review, which was published in 2018. Epilepsy is a neurological condition that affects over 70 million individuals globally. Among these, nearly 25% of patients experience drug-resistant epilepsy, a condition where seizures persist despite treatment with antiepileptic medications. Drug-resistant epilepsy is associated with an increased risk of premature death, physical injuries, psychosocial challenges, and a diminished quality of life. The objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and tolerability of clonazepam as an add-on therapy for both adults and children with drug-resistant focal onset or generalized onset epileptic seizures. This evaluation compared clonazepam to either a placebo or another antiepileptic drug. For the most recent update, a comprehensive search was conducted on June 4, 2019, across several databases, including the Cochrane Register of Studies (CRS Web), MEDLINE, Embase, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP). The search included randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials. The inclusion criteria required double-blind randomized controlled trials that investigated clonazepam as an add-on therapy for individuals with drug-resistant focal or generalized onset seizures. The minimum treatment duration for these studies was set at eight weeks, and both parallel and cross-over study designs were considered eligible. Two independent reviewers selected studies for inclusion, extracted relevant data, and assessed the quality of the trials. Efforts were made to contact study authors for additional information when necessary. However, no double-blind randomized controlled trials meeting the inclusion criteria were identified. As a result, there is no evidence from such trials to support or refute the use of clonazepam as an add-on therapy for drug-resistant focal or generalized onset epileptic seizures in adults or children. Since the last version of this review, no new studies have been found.
